Nigeria's Constitution, in plain English
Ask about your rights.Get the exact section.
Type your question the way you would say it. We find the part of the Constitution that answers it, explain it in plain English and show you the official wording beside it.
- Free to use
- No account needed
- Every answer cites its section
Why it is hard
The Constitution is written for lawyers. Your question is not.
It runs to 320 sections and 7 schedules of formal legal English. The words you would search for are rarely the words it uses.
Searching the PDF
You search for “phone”. Nothing comes up.
The section you need talks about “telephone conversations and telegraphic communications”, and the limits on it sit eight sections later.
With constitution.ng
You ask “can police search my phone?”
Section 37 comes first, Section 45 comes with it for the limits, and the answer explains both in two sentences.
The Constitution belongs to every Nigerian. Now every Nigerian can read it.
What you get
Answers you can understand and check
- Ask in your own words Plain English, Pidgin or a half remembered section number. “Section thirty something about privacy” still finds Section 37.
- The answer comes first You get a direct reply to what you asked, then what it means for you and where the limits are. No legal jargon to decode.
- The official wording, every time Every answer shows the exact text of the sections it relies on, with citations taken from the Constitution itself.
- Keep what you find Copy an answer with its citations, save sections for later, or open the page in the printed source to check it yourself.
How it works
Three steps, about ten seconds
- 01 Ask your question Type it as you would ask a friend who knows the law. A section number works too.
- 02 We find the sections Your question is matched against all 320 sections and 7 schedules, including the ones that limit a right.
- 03 Read the answer and the source A short answer in plain English, with the official wording of each section right beside it.
Built to be checked
Tested on the questions people really ask
We measure every change against real phrasing, not legal phrasing. Here is where it stands today.

Questions
Before you ask
The short version: it is free, it is independent, and it always shows you the source.
Is this legal advice?
No. constitution.ng explains what the Constitution says and shows you the exact section. If you are facing a court case, an arrest or a dispute, speak to a lawyer or the Legal Aid Council. Bring the sections you found here with you.
Is it free?
Yes. Asking questions, finding sections and reading the full Constitution are free. There is no paid plan.
Do I need an account?
No. You can ask and read as a guest. Create an account only if you want your conversations to follow you to another device.
Is this the current Constitution?
It is the 1999 Constitution as published in 2004. Amendments passed after that are not included yet, so a section may have changed since. Every answer tells you this so you can check before you rely on it.
Can I ask in Pidgin?
Yes. Ask the way you would say it, in English or Pidgin, and we will find the section. Answers are written in plain English, and the official wording is always the English text.
How do you choose the section?
Your question is matched against every section, using both the words you typed and what you mean. Citations come from the text itself, never guessed, and every answer lists the sections it used so you can read them yourself.
Can I quote an answer?
Yes. Copy any answer with its citations, or save the sections you need. Quote the official wording, not the explanation, when accuracy matters.
Is this a government website?
No. constitution.ng is independent. It is not published by, or connected to, the National Assembly or any government body.
